title: Sparkling, sweet, fortified, beer, sake, spirits and cocktails
lead: The Certified view of everything beyond still wine: Champagne in detail, the world's sparkling methods, sweet and fortified wines, beer and sake, spirits and liqueurs, and the Court's 33 cocktails.

intro.title: WHAT CERTIFIED ADDS
intro.text: Level 1 taught what each drink is. The Certified exam asks for methods, styles, iconic producers, aging rules and pairings, plus every listed cocktail's base, mixers and garnish.

sections.name: Champagne in depth

lines.label: Place
lines.text: Cool continental, near the 49th parallel, with no shelter from Atlantic weather: rain, frost and hail are threats. Grapes are picked early to keep their acidity.

lines.label: The map
lines.text: The Court lists five areas: Montagne de Reims, Vallée de la Marne, Côte des Blancs, Côte de Sézanne and Côte des Bar.

know: Liqueur de tirage is wine, sugar and yeast. Liqueur d'expédition is wine and cane sugar.
Non-vintage needs 15 months (12 on the lees); vintage needs 36 months.
17 villages keep the Grand Cru name and 42 keep Premier Cru, from the old Échelle des Crus.
Côte des Blancs is Chardonnay country; in the Côte des Bar, 83% of vines are Pinot Noir.
Spécial Club is the top cuvée of the Club Trésors growers' group, founded in 1971.

sections.name: Sweet wines

lines.label: Three ways
lines.text: Noble rot (Sauternes, Tokaji Aszú, Alsace SGN, German BA and TBA, Loire Chenin), drying (Vin Santo, Recioto) and freezing (Eiswein, Icewine). Eiswein and Icewine must be free of noble rot.

sections.name: Sherry

lines.label: Place
lines.text: Southwest Spain: Jerez-Xérès-Sherry, with Sanlúcar de Barrameda on the coast. Hot maritime climate; albariza (chalk) is the prized soil, with barros (clay) and arenas (sand).

lines.label: Method
lines.text: Fortified after fermentation. Wines under flor (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) age biologically; the rest age oxidatively. All age in the solera.

know: Fino and Manzanilla are fortified to 15%; Oloroso to at least 17%, which stops flor.
Palo Cortado starts under flor, is re-fortified above 17%, then ages oxidatively.
Running the scales: draw from the solera, refill it from the 1st criadera, and so on up.
The Court lists Manzanilla, Fino, Amontillado and Palo Cortado as biological; Oloroso and Cream as oxidative.
Serve Fino chilled, at 6-8°C.

sections.name: Port, Madeira and other fortified wines

lines.label: Port
lines.text: Same area as the Douro DOP: Baixo Corgo, Cima Corgo, Douro Superior. Schist slopes, warm to hot Mediterranean climate. Fortified during fermentation; Vila Nova de Gaia is the Port term to know.

lines.label: Madeira
lines.text: A volcanic island near North Africa; Funchal is the main city. Fortified during fermentation, then heated and oxidized: estufagem (tanks) or canteiro (casks).

know: Ruby family: Ruby, LBV, Single Quinta, Vintage. Aged Tawny: 10, 20, 30, 40 years; Colheita at least 7 years.
Vintage Port is only made in the best years; old Vintage and Single Quinta Ports need decanting.
Estufagem: 45-50°C for at least 3 months. Canteiro: in casks, usually upstairs, for at least 2 years.
Madeira, driest to sweetest: Sercial, Verdelho, Bual, Malmsey. Tinta Negra is also used.

sections.name: Beer and sake

lines.label: Beer
lines.text: Germination and kilning make the malt; mashing and boiling come next; lagers get a cold lagering rest. Ales use S. cerevisiae (68-72°F), lagers S. pastorianus (48-55°F).

lines.label: Sake
lines.text: Koji (Aspergillus oryzae) and yeast work at the same time: parallel fermentation. Premium grades depend on how much of the rice grain is left.

know: American hops: Cascade, Centennial, Citra. European hops: Hallertau, Saaz, Tettnang.
Daiginjo keeps 50% of the grain or less, Ginjo 60%, Honjozo 70%. Junmai means no added alcohol.
Sake Meter Value runs about -15 to +15; the higher, the drier.
Sake bottles: 300 ml, 720 ml, 1.8 L.
A quarter-barrel keg holds 992 oz (29.3 L); a pint is 16 oz.

sections.name: Clear and agave spirits

lines.label: Where
lines.text: Vodka, gin and rum can be made anywhere; rum is traditionally Caribbean. Tequila is Jalisco and blue agave. Mezcal is Oaxaca, from many agaves, roasted in pits for a smoky note.

lines.label: Aging
lines.text: Tequila: Blanco straight from the still, Reposado 2 months to 1 year in oak, Añejo 1-3 years, Extra Añejo 3 years or more.

know: US vodka is distilled to 95% ABV or more and never aged in wood.
Gin must taste mainly of juniper; 'London' and 'Dry' are for distilled gin only.
Tequila uses only blue agave; '100% agave' is bottled in Mexico, plain 'Tequila' needs 51%.
Cachaça is Brazil's sugarcane rum, the base of a Caipirinha.
Mezcal producers on the Court's list: Bozal, Del Maguey, Wahaka.

mixups.why: Tirage (wine, sugar, yeast) starts the bubbles. Expédition (wine, cane sugar) is the dosage after disgorging.

Junmai has no added alcohol. Honjozo adds a little, up to 10% of the rice weight.

facts.fact: Certified column: Champagne sits on the 49th parallel, one of the most northerly wine regions; cool continental climate; no protection from Atlantic influence, so unpredictable weather, rain, frost and hail threats; Marne River; limestone and chalk soils; grapes are picked earlier to preserve natural acidity.
Certified column: Champagne AOP subregions: Vallée de la Marne, Côte des Blancs, Montagne de Reims, Côte des Bar, Côte de Sézanne.

Comité Champagne: four main sub-regions: Montagne de Reims (around Reims, most common grape Pinot noir), Marne Valley (east near Épernay mainly Pinot noir, Meunier dominant moving west), Côte des Blancs (named for Chardonnay; chalk cliffs well suited to Chardonnay) and Côte des Bar (south-east of Troyes; Pinot noir 83% of vines).
Certified column: plantings 38% Pinot Noir, 32% Meunier, 30% Chardonnay.

Certified column (Champagne): know the contents of liqueur de tirage and of liqueur d'expédition and how the latter affects the style of the wine. Steps: still wine is made; assemblage of cuvée; bubbles created using liqueur de tirage; sur lie aging - autolysis; riddling (remuage) using pupitre or gyropalette; disgorging (dégorgement); dosage added using liqueur d'expédition.
Comité Champagne glossary: liqueur de tirage is a solution of yeasts, sugar and wine added to the cuvée to trigger the second fermentation in the bottle.

Comité Champagne glossary: immediately after disgorgement the bottle is topped up with a dosage liqueur (liqueur d'expédition), a mixture of cane sugar and wine, the quantity of which varies according to the style of Champagne.

Comité Champagne: during maturation on lees the dead yeasts decompose (autolysis) while minute quantities of oxygen enter, causing slow oxidation; cellars at a steady temperature of around 12°C; in practice non-vintage is aged 2-3 years and vintage 4-10 years.
Certified column: non-vintage 12 months on lees, minimum 15 months total; vintage minimum 36 months total aging.

Comité Champagne: manual riddling uses wooden pupitres, turning each bottle 1/8 or 1/4 turn; it takes 4-6 weeks and about 25 turns per bottle. Automated riddling machines (gyropalettes) handle metal racks of 500 bottles and take about one week instead of six.

Comité Champagne: for disgorgement the bottle neck is plunged into a solution at about -27°C, forming a frozen plug of sediment that the bottle's pressure expels when opened; large bottles and some cuvées are still disgorged by hand ('à la volée').
Comité Champagne: 17 crus have kept the Grand Cru designation and 42 the Premier Cru designation. The old échelle des crus rated villages 80-100%; it was scrapped in 2010 but villages kept the terms.
Certified column: Échelle des Crus: Grand Cru villages and Premier Cru villages exist and may be put on labels.

Certified column (Champagne): label terms Special Club, Récoltant Manipulant, Négociant Manipulant, Vieilles Vignes; general terms Cuvée de Prestige / Tête de Cuvée, Grandes Marques, single vineyard, Clos. Be able to match Grandes Marques to their prestige cuvées; know three non-Grandes Marques producers and three grower producers; know the best vintages going back 15 years.
Comité Champagne: label codes include NM (Négociant-Manipulant, buys grapes or wine; all the big houses) and RM (Récoltant-Manipulant, a grower using only their own grapes).
Club Trésors de Champagne: founded in 1971, the first association of Champagne grower-producers, committed to a wine of excellence, the Spécial Club cuvée.

LVMH (Veuve Clicquot): Madame Clicquot created the first vintage champagne in 1810, invented the riddling table in 1816 and produced the first blended rosé champagne in 1818; La Grande Dame is one of the house's iconic cuvées.
LVMH (Krug): Krug Grande Cuvée blends 120+ wines from more than 10 different years; Le Clos du Mesnil is a 1.84-hectare Krug plot in Mesnil-sur-Oger.
Louis Roederer's own site lists Cristal and Cristal Rosé among the house's wines.
Certified column: history and lore: invention of the riddling rack (Madame Clicquot) and the gyropalette.

Champagne service (Court): never point the cork at someone and never take your hand off the top (cage and cork) while removing the cork; CMS-A published sparkling wine opening standards; Champagne is an incredibly versatile beverage that goes with many types of foods.

Certified column (World Sparkling): traditional method steps; know what liqueur de tirage and liqueur d'expédition are made of; examples include Cap Classique. Intro column examples: Champagne, Crémant, Cava, Franciacorta.
Cap Classique Producers Association: Cap Classique is the classic method of making sparkling wine by creating a second fermentation in the bottle; the term has been used since 1992.

Charmat (cuve close): second fermentation in pressurized tanks, complete in 4-5 days; filtered then bottled; saves time and cost with no riddling or disgorging; as little as 90 days from harvest to bottling; best process for aromatic grape varieties; examples Prosecco, Moscato d'Asti; Certified column adds Lambrusco.

Transfer method: identical to the classic method up to the end of the second fermentation in bottle; bottles are disgorged under pressure into large tanks, filtered and rebottled; lees contact is obtained and riddling eliminated; used for extra large and extra small bottles.

Méthode ancestrale: primary fermentation paused mid-way, wine bottled, fermentation finishes in bottle trapping CO2; no requirement to disgorge. Certified: also called Ancestral Method / Méthode Rurale / Pétillant Naturel ('pet-nat'); bottled at much lower pressure.

Certified label term: Crémant is French sparkling wine made by méthode traditionnelle outside the Champagne region, e.g. Crémant de Bourgogne, Crémant d'Alsace, Crémant de Loire. General term: gyropalette - understand its importance for time, cost and efficacy.

Certified (World Sparkling): differences between possible pairings depending on the method; impact of the cost of the various styles and how they fit a well-rounded wine program by the bottle and by the glass to offer many price points.
Certified (Alsace, BOS): Crémant d'Alsace is an alternative, cost-effective source for traditional method sparkling wine.
Cava categories by aging: Cava de Guarda minimum 9 months; Reserva more than 18 months; Gran Reserva 30 months; Cava de Paraje Calificado more than 36 months.
Franciacorta minimum time on the lees from tirage to disgorging: Franciacorta 18 months; Rosé and Satèn 24; vintage (millesimato) 30; riserva 60.

Sweet wines: noble rot appellations - Bordeaux: Sauternes; Alsace: VT and SGN; Germany: Auslese, BA, TBA; Loire: Quarts de Chaume, Bonnezeaux, Vouvray Moelleux; Hungary: Tokaji Aszú. Drying - Italy: Vin Santo, Recioto di Soave, Recioto della Valpolicella. Freezing - Germany & Austria: Eiswein; Canada: Icewine (Ontario VQA). Certified: match appellations with their regions and grapes; Eiswein and Icewine must be free of noble rot.

Sweet wine grapes: Sauternes Sémillon; Alsace Riesling, Pinot Gris, Gewürztraminer, Muscat; Loire Chenin Blanc; Tokaji Furmint. Certified: Vin Santo Trebbiano; Recioto di Soave Garganega; Recioto della Valpolicella Corvina; Canada Vidal, Riesling, Cabernet Franc.

Certified (Sweet): Noble Rot = Botrytis cinerea; Classification of Sauternes (1855): Château d'Yquem, Superior First Growth (Premier Cru Supérieur); know a couple of producers in each category; by-the-glass serving usually 2 oz; open bottles typically last a week kept cold in the refrigerator; match the weight of the dessert and the wine, the wine sweeter than the dessert; contrast sweet wines with fatty and salty foods such as foie gras and blue cheese; really old wines become drier over time; many are in clear bottles and should be kept out of direct light; full-sized bottles age better than half bottles; Tokaji is often bottled in 500ml bottles, cost by the glass correctly.
Tokaj: since 2013, 120 g/l is the minimum residual sugar for Aszú; 6 puttony means upwards of 150 g/l; Aszú must age at least 18 months in wooden casks.
Ontario VQA Icewine: grapes frozen naturally on the vine, harvested below -8°C, juice at least 35 degrees Brix.

Certified (Fortified): Sherry appellation Jerez-Xérès-Sherry, with Sanlúcar de Barrameda on the coast; climate hot maritime; close to the Atlantic; soils albariza (chalk), barros (clay), arenas (sand); fortified after fermentation, oxidized; flor: Saccharomyces cerevisiae; biological aging vs oxidative aging; running the scales of the solera; grapes Palomino, Moscatel, Pedro Ximénez.
Certified (Sherry style): biological aging - Manzanilla, Fino, Amontillado, Palo Cortado; oxidative aging - Oloroso, Cream Sherry.
Sherry: wines classified for fino and manzanilla are fortified to 15% ABV; wines for oloroso to at least 17%.

Sherry solera: wine is drawn (saca) from the solera, the oldest tier; it is topped up (rocío) from the 1st criadera, and so on up to the youngest tier, which is topped up with new wine; the whole process is called correr escalas (running the scales).
Biological ageing happens under a film of yeasts (velo de flor) that protects the wine from oxidation; oxidative ageing exposes the wine to oxygen, darkening and concentrating it.
Albariza is a white soil of chalk and clay, the best soil for Palomino.
Fino: dry white wine from Palomino, aged under flor; serve chilled 6-8°C.
Manzanilla: dry Palomino wine aged under flor; its biological ageing must happen entirely in bodegas in Sanlúcar de Barrameda.
Amontillado ages first under flor; then the flor disappears and the wine ages oxidatively.
Oloroso is fortified to 17%, which prevents flor, so it ages in contact with oxygen.

Palo Cortado: very fine must initially fortified to 15%, casks marked with a 'palo'; casks showing specific traits are marked as potential Palo Cortado and re-fortified above 17%, redirecting the wine to oxidative ageing; it combines the delicate bouquet of an Amontillado with the body of an Oloroso.
Pedro Ximénez is made from overripe grapes dried in the sun; fermentation is stopped with wine alcohol; ageing is exclusively oxidative; sugar more than 212 g/l.

Certified (Fortified): by-the-glass pours typically 2 oz; refer to the CMS Hospitality and Service Standards for service temperatures; understand how sweetness, age and oxidation affect pairings; know general shelf life after opening.

Certified (Port): same area as the Douro DOP, Portugal; subregions Cima Corgo, Baixo Corgo, Douro Superior; warm to hot Mediterranean; mountainous hillside; schist; fortified during fermentation; general term Vila Nova de Gaia; Ruby: basic Ruby, LBV, Single Quinta, Vintage; Aged Tawny 10, 20, 30, 40-year; Colheita (min 7 years aging); grape Touriga Nacional.
Certified: vintage Port is only made in the best vintages; old Vintage and Single Quinta Ports require decanting for sediment.
IVDP: Port fermentation is stopped by adding grape brandy (benefício); Port usually has 19-22% alcohol; sweetness depends on when the brandy is added.

IVDP: LBV is a Ruby Port from a single year bottled after four to six years in wood; Vintage Port is bottled two to three years after the vintage and is the only Port that ages in bottle; Single Quinta Vintage comes from a single harvest and a single estate (quinta); Colheita is a single-vintage Tawny aged in cask at least seven years.

Certified (Madeira): Funchal is the main city; hot subtropical; mountainous hillside; volcanic soil; fortified during fermentation, oxidized, exposed to heat; know estufagem and canteiro; sweeter styles are fortified closer to the beginning of fermentation; grapes Sercial, Verdelho, Bual, Malmsey, Tinta Negra; driest to sweetest: Sercial, Verdelho, Bual, Malmsey.

Madeira: fortification with 96% wine alcohol stops fermentation; estufagem heats the wine in stainless steel tanks at 45-50°C for at least 3 months; canteiro ages it in casks, usually on the warmer upper floors, for at least 2 years. (Translated.)
Madeira cannot be bottled before 3 years old; age indications 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 50 and over 50 years. (Translated.)

Certified (Fortified): Marsala DOC, Sicily, styles Secco, Semi-Secco, Dolce; French fortified: Banyuls AOP (Roussillon, Grenache), Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise AOP (Southern Rhône, Muscat); other: Rutherglen, Victoria, Australia (Muscat); Klein Karoo, Western Cape, South Africa (Muscat de Frontignan and Muscat à Petits Grains).
Winemakers of Rutherglen: Muscat of Rutherglen is classified in four tiers - Rutherglen, Classic, Grand, Rare - marking a progression in richness, complexity, age and intensity.
Certified (Beer) learning outcome statement: recommend producers of specific styles of beer, choose the appropriate glass for specific beers, and answer beer costing scenarios.

Certified (Beer): germination - grain kernels produce enzymes that turn starches into sugar, creating malt; kilning - heating germinated barley to dry it and develop flavor and color; time and temperature determine color and flavor.
Certified (Beer): ales Saccharomyces cerevisiae, warm and fast fermentation (68-72°F / 20-22°C); lagers Saccharomyces pastorianus, cool and slow fermentation (48-55°F / 9-13°C).
Certified (Beer): American hops Cascade, Centennial, Citra; European hops Hallertau, Saaz, Tettnang; water's mineral and ion content shapes the style produced.

Certified (Beer): process terms mashing, boiling, lagering; ABV = alcohol by volume; IBU = International Bitterness Unit, higher means more bitter. Producer examples: recall at least two producers of common styles (European and American pale lager, Pilsner, American IPA, American Pale Ale, porter, Irish dry stout, Hefeweizen, Witbier, sour).

Certified (Beer): beer is one of the oldest alcoholic beverages; in Mesopotamia hunter-gatherers settled to grow crops for bread and beer; glassware must be clean and polished; common glasses pint, mug, tulip, pilsner, weizen; pairing principles: sweetness from malt, bitterness from hops, generally low alcohol, carbonation; FIFO for restocking; containers bottle, can, keg; a quarter barrel keg = 29.3 litres / 992 ounces; one pint = 16 ounces.

Intro (Beer): ales are top-fermenting with more fruit and spice aromas (e.g. Hefeweizen, Pale Ale, IPA, Porter, Irish Dry Stout); lagers are bottom-fermenting, clean and crisp (e.g. Pilsner, Bock, Oktoberfest).
Business of the Sommelier: amount of bottles needed = (number of guests x oz or ml per guest) / 25 (oz in a 750 ml bottle).
Certified (Sake): Koji-kin = Aspergillus oryzae; parallel fermentation; Nigori = cloudy; Namazake = unpasteurized; Kimoto and Yamahai: no lactic acid added, resulting in a gamey flavor.

Certified (Sake): premium classification based on minimum % of rice grain remaining: Daiginjo 50%, Ginjo 60%, Honjozo 70%; no alcohol added: Junmai Daiginjo 50%, Junmai Ginjo 60%; Sake Meter Value: the higher the number the drier, range -15 to +15; Tokubetsu = special sake category; Ginjo and Daiginjo best chilled; lower polishing levels, Yamahai and Kimoto chilled or warm; Kimoto and Yamahai have more umami for bigger, richer meats; bottle sizes 300ml / 720ml / 1.8L.

JSS glossary: kimoto acquires acidity by cultivating wild lactic acid bacteria, grinding rice and koji together; yamahai does the same without the grinding; both tend to be full-bodied. Sokujo, the modern method, simply adds lactic acid.

JSS glossary: Honjozo uses rice polished to 70% or less plus neutral spirits up to 10% of the polished rice weight; Junmai is made without neutral spirits; specially designated sake has 8 categories; namazake is unpasteurized and best stored in the fridge; nigori is cloudy sake filtered with a coarse mesh.

Court spirits table (clear and agave): Vodka - anywhere, commonly cereal grain but can be anything, commonly continuous still, distilled multiple times to remove flavors; producers Tito's, Absolut, Smirnoff, Stolichnaya, Grey Goose, Ketel One, Cîroc, Belvedere. Rum - traditionally Caribbean, sugarcane and molasses, continuous or pot still; styles Light, Dark, Aged, Spiced; producers Myers's, Mount Gay, Bacardi, Captain Morgan (spiced), Diplomático, Goslings, Havana Club. Gin - anywhere, neutral grain, continuous, botanicals and juniper; London Dry; Tanqueray, Bombay, Nolet, Beefeater, Hendrick's, Sipsmith. Tequila - Jalisco, blue agave; Blanco under 2 months, Reposado 2 months to 1 year in oak, Añejo 1 to 3 years in oak; Don Julio, Jose Cuervo, Patrón, Herradura, Sauza, El Jimador, 1800, Hornitos. Mezcal - Oaxaca, many agave varieties, agave cooked over fire in pits gives a smoky character; Blanco most common, Reposado, Añejo; Bozal, Del Maguey, Wahaka.
US rules: vodka is neutral spirit distilled at or above 95% ABV and may not be aged or stored in wood.
US rules: gin must derive its main characteristic flavor from juniper berries; only gin made by original distillation or redistillation may be called 'distilled', 'Dry', 'London' or 'Old Tom'.
US rules: rum is distilled from sugar cane juice, syrup, molasses or other cane by-products; Cachaça is rum that is a distinctive product of Brazil.
CRT: only blue agave (Agave tequilana Weber) is permitted; the appellation covers 181 municipalities in five states: Jalisco, Michoacán, Guanajuato, Nayarit and Tamaulipas.

CRT: Tequila 100% Agave is made from 100% blue agave sugars and bottled at origin; 'Tequila' needs at least 51% blue agave sugars and may be bottled outside the territory; Blanco comes direct from the still; Reposado at least 2 months in oak, añejo at least 1 year, extra añejo at least 3 years.

Court spirits table (whisk(e)y): Bourbon - USA, most made in Kentucky but not required, 51% corn, typically continuous, new charred American white oak; Jim Beam, Maker's Mark, Wild Turkey, Bulleit, Buffalo Trace, Woodford Reserve. Tennessee - 51% corn, filtered through maple charcoal; Jack Daniel's, George Dickel. Canadian - corn, wheat, rye or barley; Crown Royal, Pike Creek, Canadian Club. Irish - barley, three times in pot still; Jameson, Tullamore Dew, Bushmills, Proper Twelve. Scotch - barley; Highland, Lowland, Islay (smokiest), Speyside, Campbeltown; min 3 years in oak; single malt / blended; two times in pot still, Lowlands three; peat fires dry the barley giving a smoky character; Highland/Speyside: The Glenlivet, Macallan, Singleton, Glenmorangie; Lowland: Glenkinchie, Auchentoshan; Islay: Lagavulin, Laphroaig (spelled 'Laphroig' in the guide), Ardbeg, Bowmore, Caol Ila; blended: Johnnie Walker, Ballantine's, Chivas, Grant's, Famous Grouse, J&B, Dewar's.

UK Scotch Whisky Regulations: Scotch matured only in Scotland in oak casks for at least three years; Single Malt is from one distillery, water and malted barley only, pot stills; Blended Scotch blends single malt(s) with single grain(s).

Court spirits table (brandy): Cognac - subregions Grande Champagne, Petite Champagne (Fine Champagne); VS/Three Star 2 years, VSOP 4, XO 10; white grapes mainly Ugni Blanc; two times in a pot still; aged in French oak; Hennessy, Rémy Martin, Courvoisier, Martell. Armagnac - Haut Armagnac, Bas Armagnac, Ténarèze; VS 2, VSOP 4, XO 10; Ugni Blanc, Folle Blanche, Colombard, Baco; one time in a unique continuous still; French oak; Larressingle, Delord, Montal. Calvados - apples, pears; min 2 years in oak; two times in pot still, some continuous. Eaux de vie de fruits - Framboise, Kirsch, Poire William (raspberry, cherry, pear), generally no aging. Pomace brandy - Grappa (Italy), Marc (France), generally no aging.
BNIC: 'Fine Champagne' Cognac is a blend of Grande Champagne (minimum 50%) and Petite Champagne; XXO means 14 years or more.

Court liqueurs table: Herb & Nut - Bénédictine, B&B, Pimm's, Chartreuse, Crème de Menthe, Frangelico; Anise - Anisette, Galliano, Ouzo, Sambuca; Fruit - Orange: Triple Sec, Cointreau, Grand Marnier; Apricot: Amaretto; Peaches: Southern Comfort; Cream - Baileys Irish Cream; Whiskey - Drambuie, Glayva, Irish Mist; Other - Elderflower: St. Germain; Ginger: Canton; Coffee: Kahlúa, Tia Maria.
US rules: cordials and liqueurs are flavored spirits made with fruits, flowers, plants or other natural flavors, with at least 2.5% sugar by weight.

read.stopsTitle: The traditional method, step by step

stops.name: Cuvée and tirage
stops.text: Still wines are blended into the **cuvée**. The **liqueur de tirage** (wine, sugar and yeast) goes in to start the second fermentation in the bottle.

stops.name: Lees aging
stops.text: Dead yeast breaks down (**autolysis**) while a trace of oxygen gets in, in cellars around 12°C. Non-vintage needs **15 months** (12 on the lees); vintage **36 months**.

stops.name: Riddling
stops.text: By hand on wooden **pupitres** it takes 4-6 weeks and about 25 turns. A **gyropalette** turns 500 bottles at once in about a week.

stops.name: Disgorging
stops.text: The neck is frozen in a bath near -27°C and the pressure pushes the ice plug out. Big bottles are still done by hand (**à la volée**).

stops.name: Dosage
stops.text: Wine and cane sugar top up the bottle. The amount of sugar sets the style, from Brut Nature to Doux.

read.bigIdea: The method sets the style and the price.
read.where: From Level 1: the four methods. Now tie each one to its wines. The traditional method makes **Champagne**, **Crémant**, **Cava**, **Franciacorta** and South Africa's **Cap Classique**. A good list offers several methods and price points, by the glass and by the bottle. **Crémant d'Alsace** is a cost-effective traditional-method choice.

stops.name: Traditional
stops.text: The slow, costly way: lees aging, riddling and disgorging in each bottle. The **gyropalette** saves time and cost in riddling.

stops.name: Charmat
stops.text: The second fermentation runs in a pressure tank in 4-5 days, with no riddling or disgorging. It suits aromatic grapes: **Prosecco**, **Moscato d'Asti**, **Lambrusco**.

stops.name: Transfer
stops.text: Ferments in bottle, then is emptied into a tank under pressure, filtered and rebottled. Lees contact, no riddling. Used for very large and very small bottles.

stops.name: Ancestral
stops.text: The first fermentation is paused, and finishes in the bottle. Lower pressure, and no need to disgorge. Also called **méthode rurale**.

read.mixup: **Crémant** is French traditional method from outside Champagne. **Cava** is Spain's traditional-method DO.
read.sayIt: Crémant is made the same way as Champagne and usually costs less.

read.stopsTitle: From driest and palest to sweetest

stops.name: Fino and Manzanilla
stops.text: Palomino fortified to 15% and aged under **flor**. Manzanilla must age in **Sanlúcar de Barrameda**. Serve Fino chilled.

stops.name: Amontillado
stops.text: Starts under flor. When the flor dies, it carries on aging in contact with oxygen.

stops.name: Palo Cortado
stops.text: Starts at 15% under flor. The cellar marks the cask and re-fortifies it above 17%. Amontillado's delicacy with Oloroso's body.

stops.name: Oloroso
stops.text: Fortified to **17%**, so no flor grows. It ages in contact with oxygen and darkens.

stops.name: Cream and PX
stops.text: The Court lists **Cream** as oxidative. **Pedro Ximénez** comes from sun-dried grapes, with over 212 g/L of sugar.

read.mixup: **Amontillado** loses its flor naturally. **Palo Cortado** is re-fortified on purpose, above 17%.

read.bigIdea: Fortified during or after fermentation sets the style.
read.where: From Level 1: Port's Ruby and Tawny families, and Madeira's four grapes. Port and Madeira are both fortified **during** fermentation, so some grape sugar stays. Port comes from the **Douro**: **Baixo Corgo**, **Cima Corgo** and **Douro Superior**, on schist. **Madeira** is a volcanic island, and its wine is heated and oxidized on purpose.
read.stopsTitle: Port, then Madeira, then the rest

stops.name: Ruby Port
stops.text: **LBV** is one year, bottled after 4-6 years in wood. **Vintage** is bottled after 2-3 years and ages in bottle. **Single Quinta** is one year from one estate.

stops.name: Tawny Port
stops.text: Aged Tawny says **10, 20, 30 or 40** years. **Colheita** is a one-year Tawny with at least 7 years in cask.

stops.name: Madeira
stops.text: Wine alcohol (96%) stops the fermentation; earlier means sweeter. Then **estufagem** (45-50°C tanks) or **canteiro** (casks). No bottling before 3 years.

stops.name: Rutherglen Muscat
stops.text: Four tiers: **Rutherglen, Classic, Grand, Rare**, each richer and older than the last.

read.bigIdea: Certified adds the steps, the glass and the grade.
read.where: From Level 1: malt, hops, yeast and water; ale versus lager; sake's main grades. Beer is one of the oldest drinks: in **Mesopotamia**, early farmers grew grain for bread and beer. The Court now wants brewing steps, glassware, producers and keg math for beer, and polishing grades, styles and service for sake.

stops.name: Malt
stops.text: Sprouting grain makes enzymes that turn starch into sugar (**germination**). **Kilning** dries it; time and heat set the color and flavor.

stops.name: Brew
stops.text: **Mashing** and **boiling** come before fermentation. Lagers then rest cold (**lagering**). Local water minerals shape the style.

stops.name: Serve beer
stops.text: Know the **pint, mug, tulip, pilsner and weizen** glasses. Malt sweetness, hop bitterness, low alcohol and bubbles make beer easy with food. Restock first in, first out (**FIFO**).

stops.name: Sake styles
stops.text: **Kimoto** and **yamahai** grow wild lactic bacteria instead of adding lactic acid; yamahai skips the grinding. Both are fuller, with more umami for rich meats.

stops.name: Serve sake
stops.text: **Ginjo** and **Daiginjo** are best chilled. Lower grades, kimoto and yamahai can be chilled or warm. **Nigori** is cloudy; **namazake** is unpasteurized, so keep it cold.

read.bigIdea: Clear spirits differ by raw material and rules.
read.where: From Level 1: what each spirit is made from. Now add the styles, the aging rules and the producers. Vodka, gin and rum can be made anywhere. **Tequila** and **mezcal** must come from Mexico: the Court places Tequila in **Jalisco** and mezcal in **Oaxaca**.

stops.name: Vodka
stops.text: Usually grain, but it can be anything. Distilled many times in a column still to strip out flavor.

stops.name: Gin
stops.text: Neutral grain spirit flavored with juniper and botanicals. **London Dry** is the style the Court names.

stops.name: Rum
stops.text: Cane juice or molasses, in a column or pot still. Styles: **light, dark, aged, spiced**. Brazil's cachaça is a rum.

stops.name: Tequila
stops.text: Only blue agave, from an appellation covering parts of five Mexican states. **Blanco, Reposado, Añejo, Extra Añejo.**

stops.name: Mezcal

read.bigIdea: Aged spirits are about grain or grape, still and oak.
read.where: From Level 1: what each whiskey and brandy is made from. Now add regions, aging rules and producers, the way you'd sell them. Then sort the liqueurs by family, so you can recommend one fast.

stops.name: American
stops.text: **Bourbon** is 51% corn in new charred oak; most is from Kentucky, but it doesn't have to be. **Tennessee** whiskey is filtered through maple charcoal: Jack Daniel's, George Dickel.

stops.name: Irish and Canadian
stops.text: **Irish** is barley, distilled three times in pot stills (Jameson, Bushmills). **Canadian** uses corn, wheat, rye or barley (Crown Royal, Canadian Club).

stops.name: Scotch
stops.text: At least 3 years in oak in Scotland. Peat smoke makes **Islay** the smokiest. A single malt is one distillery; blends include Johnnie Walker and Chivas.

stops.name: Brandy
stops.text: **Cognac** is mainly Ugni Blanc, double distilled in pot stills (Hennessy, Rémy Martin). **Armagnac** goes once through a column still (Larressingle, Delord).

stops.name: Liqueurs
stops.text: Flavored spirits with at least 2.5% sugar (US rule). Learn them by family: herb, anise, orange, cream, whiskey, coffee.

read.mixup: **Cognac** is distilled twice in a pot still. **Armagnac** is distilled once in a column still.
read.sayIt: If you like smoke, try an Islay Scotch.

read.bigIdea: Learn the cocktails by their base spirit.
read.where: The Court lists **33 cocktails**, and you need each one's **base spirit**, **mixers** and **garnish**. Group them by base and they're easier to hold. Specs below follow the **IBA** official list; five drinks the IBA doesn't list follow **Difford's Guide**.

stops.name: Gin
stops.text: **Aviation, French 75, Gibson, Gimlet, Negroni, Tom Collins, John Collins, Vesper.** Tom Collins uses Old Tom gin; a Vesper adds vodka and Lillet Blanc.

stops.name: Vodka
stops.text: **Cosmopolitan, Kamikaze, French Martini, Moscow Mule, Sea Breeze, Greyhound, White Russian.** The White Russian is vodka and coffee liqueur with cream floated on top.

stops.name: Rum and cachaça

stops.name: Whiskey

court.outcome:
FRANCE - CHAMPAGNE: After studying this section, a candidate will know all the steps in the traditional method, the major regions of Champagne, and their major styles. A Certified Sommelier will and be able to speak knowledgeably about vintages over the last 10 years, recognize iconic producers, and be able to recommend and sell food pairings with wines from Champagne to a guest.

WORLD SPARKLING WINES: After studying this section, a Certified Sommelier will understand the different ways sparkling wines are made, be able to identify the method used for the world's most important sparkling wines, and describe the impact the method has on the final wine. A Certified Sommelier will be able to recommend sparkling wines to guests and pair them appropriately with food.

SWEET WINES: After studying this section, a candidate will gain a deeper knowledge of the sweet wines of the world, know iconic producers, and be able to recommend sweet wines to guests and pair them appropriately with food. Match these appellations with their larger regions and know they most common grape varieties for each.

FORTIFIED WINES: After studying this section, a candidate will understand the unique winemaking techniques used to make fortified wines. Certified Sommeliers will know iconic producers and be able to recommend and sell food pairings with fortified wines to a guest.

BEER: A Certified Sommelier will be able recommend producers of specific styles of beer to a guest, choose the appropriate glass for specific beers, and be able to accurately answer beer costing scenarios.

SAKE: After studying this section, a candidate will increase their knowledge of sake, sake styles, and polishing levels. A Certified Sommelier will be able to sell and recommend food pairings with sake to a guest.

SPIRITS & LIQUEURS: After studying this section, a candidate will gain a deeper knowledge in spirits and liqueurs of the world by understand the region, styles, raw materials, aging requirements, and the general production process. A Certified Sommelier will be able to recommend spirits and liqueurs to guests and will know the base spirits, mixers, and garnishes for selected cocktails.
